found.domain_assessment: EVIDENCE ACCESS FAILURE MUST BE READ FIRST. The session WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200 of 200) before this finder issued its first query, so zero searches ran. The egress proxy then blocked every regulator, court, ombudsman, standards-body, academic, press and vendor host attempted (gov.uk, ofgem.gov.uk, energyombudsman.org, energie-mediateur.fr, ofcom.org.uk, arcep.fr, mediation-telecom.org, faa.gov, easa.europa.eu, fmc.gov, regulations.gov, federalregister.gov, ecfr.gov, arcadis.com, procore.com, support.procore.com, autodesk.com, cassinfo.com and roughly 130 more; archives and reader proxies also blocked). Only GitHub (raw files and git clone; code search disabled for this session), npm and PyPI were reachable. Consequently no decision volume, review rate or cost figure in this cluster could be verified this session. Where I quote a number from recollection it is explicitly labelled 'recollection, unverified' with the URL that should hold it, and the verifier should treat it as a claim to check, not evidence. What WAS established from fetched primary material: (1) Procore's public API documentation describes the RFI tool as a per-project 'central storage and management point for information requests and responses' whose value is accountability and archiving; there is no cross-project 'reusable interpretation' or precedent object in its object model, and its 2026 agentic/MCP layer exposes RFIs as read/write records plus a natural-language 'converse' tool, i.e. retrieval over past RFIs rather than governed prospective settlements (github.com/procore/api-docs). (2) The DCSA container-shipping API standards model demurrage and detention only as amount and free-time fields whose meaning is 'reference to carrier website or individual charge as per service contract', confirming D&D applicability is contract-specific and negotiated, not standardised (github.com/dcsaorg/DCSA-OpenAPI). (3) Catala exists as prior art for turning legal text into executable code with lawyer ratification (github.com/CatalaLang/catala). STRUCTURAL ASSESSMENT (reasoning, not sourced numbers): The cluster contains the clearest publicly documented settlement loops of any domain (aviation: FAA exemption grants that become rule changes, EASA AltMoC notification and publication, FAA MMEL policy letters, FAA Chief Counsel legal interpretations; energy: French Mediateur national de l'energie generic recommendations that became law; maritime: FMC 2020 interpretive rule on D&D reasonableness), but in every one of these the settlement owner is a regulator or ombudsman, the settlement is already published as a versioned document, and the operating organisations consume it rather than build it. That supports H3 (already encoded) and H6 (feature of the regulator's own process), not a standalone product. At operating-company level the residual human review in this cluster is dominated by missing or conflicting information (RFIs, freight audit), factual classification (MEL applicability, container availability, meter and billing errors) and commercial negotiation (change orders, D&D, CAM), with repeatable ambiguity (H) a minority that is mostly project- or lease-local (H5). The one structurally interesting candidate is RFI resolution for repeat-programme owners (retail, data-centre, healthcare, DOT and public-housing programmes reusing standard specifications), where the same specification ambiguity plausibly recurs across projects and an owner or design firm could ratify a prospective reading; this is UNVERIFIED and sits directly in the path of Procore and Autodesk AI features and master-specification vendors. Verdict for the cluster: negative for aviation, telecom, utilities, property and logistics as standalone Sophon markets on structural grounds; uncertain for construction RFIs pending volumes and a base-rate study on real RFI logs. Absence of fetched data is uncertainty, not support; nothing here should be promoted above 'uncertain' without the blocked sources being read.

workflows.name: Construction RFIs resolved into architect's supplemental instructions and change orders
workflows.geography: US primarily (AIA A201 contract structure); UK/EU analogues under JCT/NEC/FIDIC
workflows.decision_volume: NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION. Recollection, unverified: Navigant Construction Forum 'Impact and Control of RFIs on Construction Projects' (2013) analysed roughly 1,362 projects and about 1.08 million RFIs, reporting about 9.9 RFIs per USD 1 million of construction, an average of about 796 RFIs per project, average response time about 9.7 days, and about 22 percent of RFIs never answered. URL where this should be verified: https://www.navigant.com (now guidehouse.com) construction forum publications; blocked. Source type if verified: industry consultancy study. Treat as claim to check.
workflows.human_review_rate: 100 percent by construction: every RFI is answered by a human design professional (architect or engineer of record) because the contract assigns interpretation of the contract documents to the architect (AIA A201 section 4.2.11, recollection of the clause structure, not fetched). No published share of RFIs that are answered by reference to a prior RFI was found.
workflows.why_humans_review: ESTIMATE, basis: the standard RFI taxonomies used in the industry (design clarification, conflict between drawings and specifications, missing information, substitution or alternate request, field condition, coordination clash) and the finder's reasoning; no RFI corpus was accessible. A missing evidence (information absent from drawings or specs): ~30 percent. B factual classification (does this field condition match the detail): ~10 percent. C interpretation of an existing spec or drawing where the document is ambiguous: ~20 percent. D conflict between documents (plan vs spec vs code): ~15 percent. E true discretion (aesthetic or design choice): ~5 percent. F commercial negotiation (substitutions, cost or schedule impact leading to change orders): ~10 percent. G one-off field circumstances: ~5 percent. H repeatable ambiguity settled prospectively (same spec clause questioned again on the same or a sister project): ~5 to 10 percent within a single project, potentially higher across a repeat-programme owner's portfolio. Only H is addressable and it is unverified.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Procore's public API documentation defines the RFI tool as 'a project's central storage and management point for information requests and responses' whose purpose is 'project-wide accountability' and to 'create, capture, and archive critical information exchanges'; the object model has RFIs, Specifications (with revisions) and Drawings as separate per-project objects with no precedent or reusable-interpretation entity, and the 2026 Procore AI / MCP layer exposes RFIs as records to list, search, create and update plus a free-text 'converse' tool. This is evidence that the incumbent captures RFI answers as archived per-project records, not as versioned executable settlements.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Answers are searchable text within one project; reuse across projects depends on humans remembering or searching prior projects.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Procore's agentic documentation states customers 'ask questions across their project data, drawings, RFIs, submittals' via a side-panel chat and can install AI agents that read and (with approval gate) write RFIs. Retrieval over past RFIs is therefore being shipped by the incumbent as a feature, which is the H6 threat for any RFI-precedent product.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Free-text retrieval, no ratified prospective reading.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Contractual loop (structure known, not fetched): under AIA A201 the architect's written interpretations and Architect's Supplemental Instructions apply to the project going forward and, if cost or time changes, become change orders or construction change directives; the settlement is therefore authoritative and prospective WITHIN the project but expires with the project. Repeat-programme owners and state DOTs revise standard specifications and special provisions in response to recurring RFIs and change orders, which is a cross-project loop, but no volume or frequency evidence could be fetched.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: industry association contract form (blocked, not fetched)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Within project by ASI; across projects only via periodic spec revisions, which is slow and unstructured.

workflows.economic_pain: NOT VERIFIED. Recollection, unverified: the same Navigant study estimated an average cost of about USD 1,080 per RFI to review and respond (about 8 hours of professional time), which at about 796 RFIs per project would imply roughly USD 0.86 million per project of RFI handling cost; verify at guidehouse.com or via secondary summaries (long-intl.com, blocked). Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Report figures on dispute value and duration were not fetched (arcadis.com blocked).
workflows.existing_solutions: Procore RFIs tool, Autodesk Construction Cloud (Build) RFIs, Bluebeam, Newforma, Oracle Aconex; specification systems Deltek MasterSpec/Specpoint and BSD SpecLink hold versioned spec text and are the natural home for cross-project interpretations. None captures RFI settlements as versioned executable precedents based on the Procore public docs fetched; Autodesk APS SDK on npm currently exposes only Issues and Account Admin construction packages, no RFI package (registry.npmjs.org, fetched).
workflows.buyer_and_budget: Design firm principal or owner's programme manager for repeat programmes; general contractor VDC/project controls for RFI logging. Budget is project-based and already committed to Procore or ACC seats; a standalone precedent ledger would need to be bought by the design professional who holds interpretive authority, an unusual software buyer.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: None prohibiting automation; professional liability means the licensed design professional must remain the ratifier of any interpretation, which fits the mechanism (human ratification) but caps autonomy.
workflows.notes: Best structural fit in the cluster, but locality (H5) is severe: a typical detail interpretation on one building rarely transfers to another design. The addressable pocket is repeat-programme owners with standard specs. Needs a base-rate study on one owner's RFI logs across 5 to 10 sister projects. Incumbent AI retrieval over RFIs already shipping is the main threat.

workflows.name: Energy supplier billing and tariff disputes and ombudsman complaints (UK Energy Ombudsman, Ofgem; French Mediateur national de l'energie)
workflows.decision_volume: NOT VERIFIED. The Energy Ombudsman annual report (energyombudsman.org) and the Mediateur national de l'energie rapport d'activite (energie-mediateur.fr) publish annual litige counts and category shares; both hosts blocked. No number asserted.

workflows.why_humans_review: ESTIMATE, basis: published ombudsman category structures (billing, transfers, customer service, metering) and the fact that most billing complaints concern wrong readings, estimated bills, back-billing and switching errors. A missing or wrong data ~40 percent, B factual classification ~20 percent, C rule interpretation (tariff terms, back-billing limits, standing charge applicability) ~15 percent, D conflict between licence conditions and supplier terms ~5 percent, E and G ~10 percent, F ~5 percent, H ~5 percent.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: The French Mediateur national de l'energie issues 'recommandations generiques' addressed to all operators when the same problem recurs across individual disputes; the best-known example is limitation of retroactive billing to 14 months, which was subsequently written into the Code de la consommation (article L224-11, recollection). This is a genuine prospective settlement loop: individual disputes, mediator finding, generic recommendation, operator practice change, then law. The owner is the mediator, not the supplier, and the settlement is legislation, not software. Not fetched.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Published generic recommendations and statute; suppliers encode them in billing rules.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: UK Energy Ombudsman decisions are case remedies; systemic issues are escalated to Ofgem which changes licence conditions or guidance (for example back-billing SLC and the 2017 back-billing rule, recollection). Again regulator-level, published, slow.

workflows.name: Ocean demurrage and detention (D&D) disputes and charge complaints (FMC under OSRA 2022; carrier and BCO disputes)
workflows.decision_volume: NOT VERIFIED. The FMC annual report and OSRA charge-complaint statistics would give formal and informal complaint counts; fmc.gov blocked. Container xChange and Drewry publish D&D benchmark charges; blocked. No number asserted.
workflows.human_review_rate: Disputes are negotiated between BCO or forwarder and carrier; FMC handles a small fraction.
workflows.why_humans_review: ESTIMATE: F commercial negotiation (waivers, goodwill) ~35 percent, A missing evidence (gate records, appointment availability, chassis) ~25 percent, B factual classification (who caused the delay, free time computation) ~20 percent, C interpretation of tariff and service contract free-time terms ~10 percent, D ~5 percent, H ~5 percent.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: The FMC's May 2020 Interpretive Rule on Demurrage and Detention (46 CFR 545.5) settled how the Commission assesses 'reasonableness' of D&D practices using the incentive principle, after Fact Finding 28 gathered recurring disputes; OSRA 2022 then codified invoice content requirements and shifted burden of proof, and the 2024 billing rule (46 CFR part 541) specified invoice fields. Regulator-level, published, prospective. Recollection of the regulatory sequence; not fetched.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Published interpretive rule and regulations; carriers encode invoice fields; BCOs cite the rule in disputes.

workflows.economic_pain: High aggregate (D&D charges are a major BCO cost, benchmarks not fetched), but each dispute is fact- and negotiation-heavy.
workflows.existing_solutions: Carrier billing portals, DCSA standards, D&D management vendors (Vizion, project44, Gnosis Freight), FMC CADRS and charge complaint process.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: FMC jurisdiction; carriers must keep human dispute processes.
workflows.notes: Commercial negotiation and missing facts dominate; the interpretive settlement already sits in a published FMC rule.

workflows.name: Aircraft MEL deferrals and dispatch deviations (airline maintenance control, MMEL policy letters, Dispatch Deviation Guides)
workflows.geography: US (14 CFR 91.213, 121.628), EU (EASA Part-CAT and Part-ORO MEL rules), global
workflows.decision_volume: NOT VERIFIED; airlines track open deferred defects per aircraft as an internal KPI and large carriers log thousands of deferrals per year (finder's expectation, no source). faa.gov, easa.europa.eu and skybrary.aero blocked.
workflows.human_review_rate: Each deferral is a human decision by a licensed engineer or maintenance controller applying the operator's approved MEL; 100 percent by regulation.
workflows.why_humans_review: ESTIMATE, basis: the MEL system's structure. B factual classification (is the inoperative item in the MEL, which category A/B/C/D and repair interval applies, are the (M) and (O) procedures done) ~60 percent, A missing evidence (fault confirmation) ~15 percent, C interpretation of MEL provisos ~10 percent, E operational discretion by captain and dispatcher (weather, route) ~10 percent, H ~5 percent. Interpretive ambiguity in MEL provisos is real but is resolved through the MMEL revision and policy letter process, not per airline ad hoc.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: FAA Master MEL policy letters (PLs) issued by the Flight Standards MMEL policy board record the FAA's standard relief for a class of equipment and apply prospectively to all MMELs; the Flight Operations Evaluation Board (FOEB) settles type-specific questions and revises the MMEL; operators' MELs are approved by their principal inspector. Boeing's Dispatch Deviations Guide and CDLs codify the procedures. This is a fully operating, versioned, published settlement loop owned by the regulator and OEM. Recollection of the structure; not fetched.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Published PLs and MMEL revisions; operator MEL revisions; already encoded in airline maintenance systems (AMOS, TRAX, Maintenix) as deferral categories and deadlines.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: EASA Alternative Means of Compliance (Part-ARO.GEN.120 / ORO.GEN.120): an operator proposes an AltMoC to its national authority; if accepted the NAA notifies EASA, which publishes the AltMoC list; other operators can reuse the published AltMoC only by applying to their own NAA. A published prospective settlement loop for compliance interpretations, owned by NAAs and EASA. Recollection; easa.europa.eu blocked.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Public list of accepted AltMoC; reuse still requires per-operator approval.

workflows.economic_pain: Aircraft-on-ground and delay costs are high, but the deferral decision itself is fast and rule-driven once the MEL is consulted; the pain is in the MEL/MMEL revision cycle, which is regulator-paced.
workflows.existing_solutions: AMOS, TRAX, Ramco, Maintenix for deferral tracking; FAA DRS and FSIMS for MMEL and PLs; OEM DDG and CDL manuals; EASA AltMoC list.
workflows.buyer_and_budget: Airline maintenance control and engineering; regulator flight standards. No budget line for an interpretation ledger beyond existing MRO software.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: Deferrals must be made under an approved MEL by authorised personnel; automation of the decision is not permitted beyond decision support.
workflows.notes: The strongest existence proof in the cluster that the settlement loop works, and equally strong evidence for H3: the settlements are already captured, versioned and published by the regulator and OEM, leaving factual classification at the operator.

workflows.decision_volume: NOT VERIFIED; FAA publishes exemption petitions and grants on regulations.gov dockets and a Part 107 waiver list, and the Chief Counsel interpretations database on faa.gov; all blocked. No number asserted.
workflows.human_review_rate: 100 percent; each petition is adjudicated by FAA staff.
workflows.why_humans_review: ESTIMATE: H repeatable ambiguity settled prospectively is unusually high here, perhaps ~40 percent, because petitioners routinely cite prior identical grants and the FAA issues 'summary grants' when a petition matches a previously granted one (recollection of 14 CFR part 11 practice); C interpretation ~25 percent; B factual classification of the petitioner's operation ~20 percent; G one-off ~10 percent; A ~5 percent.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Repeated identical Part 107 night-operation and operations-over-people waivers led the FAA to change the rule itself (Operations Over People and at Night final rule, effective April 2021), removing the need for the waiver class; exemption grants are cited as precedent in later grants and summary grants exist for matching petitions. This is the purest example in the cluster of ambiguity, settlement, precedent reuse, then rule change. Recollection; federalregister.gov and faa.gov blocked.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Published grants, summary grant procedure, then rulemaking.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: FAA Office of the Chief Counsel publishes legal interpretations answering regulatory questions from operators and pilots; they are searchable and are treated as authoritative guidance for future similar questions.

workflows.economic_pain: Processing backlog and petitioner delay are the pain; borne by the regulator and petitioners, not a commercial software buyer.
workflows.existing_solutions: regulations.gov, FAA DRS, internal FAA case tracking; law firms maintain exemption precedent libraries.
workflows.buyer_and_budget: The FAA (government procurement) or aviation law firms; not an enterprise software market.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: Administrative Procedure Act processes; only the agency can settle.
workflows.notes: Strong evidence that the loop exists and compounds, but the owner is a government agency and the settlements are already public and versioned, so the product would be gov-tech or a legal research tool, not the standalone enterprise product under test.

evidence_against_thesis: Every documented prospective settlement loop found in this cluster (FAA exemptions and Part 107 waivers becoming rules, EASA AltMoC publication, FAA MMEL policy letters, FMC 2020 D&D interpretive rule, Mediateur national de l'energie generic recommendations becoming statute, Ofcom General Condition changes) is owned by a regulator, ombudsman or OEM and is already captured as a versioned public document; operating companies consume these settlements, supporting H3 and H6 rather than a standalone product.

Procore's public developer documentation (fetched) treats RFIs as per-project archived question-and-answer records with accountability as the purpose, and its 2026 agentic layer adds free-text retrieval over RFIs; the incumbent is thus already shipping the 'find the prior answer' feature, and the object model has no prospective settlement entity because construction customers have not demanded one.

DCSA container-shipping standards (fetched) define demurrage and detention purely as contract-referenced amounts and free-time days, evidence that applicability is a matter of individual service contracts and negotiation (category F), not repeatable interpretive ambiguity.

Residual operator-level human review across the cluster is structurally dominated by missing or wrong data (billing complaints, freight audit references, RFI missing information), factual classification (MEL applicability, container availability, expense line classification) and commercial negotiation (change orders, D&D waivers, CAM), which supports H1 and the section 2 penalties.

Interpretations that do recur are local to a project, lease, building or service contract (H5): an RFI answer expires with the project, a lease reading binds one lease, a carrier free-time reading binds one contract.

In freight audit the mechanism is already executed inside vertical SaaS: analysts settle an accessorial question and the audit engine's contract rules are updated, so the settlement corpus is owned by the audit vendor (H3, H7).

Statutory reasonableness and discretion tests (UK s.27A service charges, French copropriete votes, captain and dispatcher authority in aviation) keep humans legally in the loop after precedent exists (H4).

refuted.claim: FAA exemption petitions / Part 107 waivers have an unusually high category H share (~40%) because petitioners cite identical prior grants and the FAA issues summary grants.
refuted.why: Category error. A petition that matches a previously granted one is not 'repeatable ambiguity': the rule is bright-line (e.g., no night operations without a waiver), the petitioner asks for discretionary relief from it (category E, routinised), and the agency's response to recurrence was to change the rule (Operations Over People and at Night final rule, effective April 2021, recollection, federalregister.gov blocked). This is exactly the IPSA pattern in prior_evidence.md: repetition is plentiful where the owner already governs with bright lines and converts recurrence into rules. Honest H share for this workflow is low (perhaps 5-10%, verifier estimate), the rest being E routinised plus B (does this operation fit the template).

The RFI product itself has an RFI-manager 'official response' that is distributed and can be attached to drawings, and RFIs carry spec-section, drawing and location references (recollection of the Procore RFI user guide; support.procore.com blocked). The api-docs object-model page is a two-sentence marketing summary, not the schema. weakened.claim: AIA A201 gives the architect authority to interpret contract documents (s.4.2.11) and ASIs apply prospectively within the project.
weakened.why: Consistent with verifier recollection (A201-2017 s.4.2.11 interpretation on written request; s.4.2.12 interpretations must be consistent with the intent of and reasonably inferable from the documents; s.4.2.13 aesthetic decisions final). But the finder marked this settlement 'prospective: yes' without noting that the architect's interpretation is contestable as a Claim under Article 15 (Initial Decision Maker, then mediation and arbitration) and that contractors routinely treat interpretations they dislike as constructive changes. So the within-project settlement is authoritative only until contested, which is H4 territory. aia.org blocked.

weakened.claim: FMC 2020 interpretive rule (46 CFR 545.5) 'settled' how reasonableness of D&D is assessed; prospective settlement loop.
weakened.why: Sequence matches verifier recollection (interpretive rule published 18 May 2020; OSRA 2022 signed 16 June 2022 adding invoice content requirements and burden shift; D&D billing final rule February 2024 at 46 CFR part 541). But the 2020 rule is expressly non-exhaustive guidance on factors the Commission 'may consider'; it preserved case-by-case adjudication of reasonableness rather than making outcomes deterministic. It is a published standard, not an executable settlement, so it supports H4 as much as it supports the loop's existence. ecfr.gov, law.cornell.edu, govinfo.gov, federalregister.gov all blocked.

weakened.claim: Mediateur national de l'energie generic recommendation on 14-month billing limit became Code de la consommation L224-11.

manual_review_conflated_with_repeatable_: Construction RFIs: finder put H at 5-10% within a project. Within-project recurrence largely collapses after the first answer because the official response or ASI is distributed to the whole team, so a second RFI on the same clause is the exception, not the rule; most RFIs are design incompleteness or coordination (A, D), design decisions (E), or contractor claim-positioning and substitution requests (F). Verifier re-estimate: H 2-5% within project, near zero cross-project except for prototype/repeat-programme owners, where the settlement already flows into prototype and master-spec revisions (H3). Basis: reasoning over standard RFI taxonomies; no corpus accessible.

FAA exemptions and Part 107 waivers: finder's H ~40% counts identical discretionary relief requests as 'repeatable ambiguity'. They are routinised waivers (E) of bright-line rules, resolved by rulemaking. Re-estimate H 5-10%, E-routinised 50%+, B 20-25%.

Aircraft MEL deferrals: finder's C 10% + H 5% treats MEL proviso reading as operator-level interpretation. Proviso ambiguity is resolved upstream by the AEG/MMEL policy process and the OEM's DDG; at the operator the residual is checklist classification (B) and operational discretion (E). Re-estimate H 0-2%.

Network charging determinations (Ofgem/CRE/ARCEP): H 10% is meaningless at tens of cases per year; each determination is the merits decision itself. H effectively 0 at organisation level; the loop is the code-modification process (H3).

Commercial lease CAM: finder gives C 40% and H 5% without explaining why house positions on a standard lease form would not recur. Some of that C is genuinely H for a large landlord with one lease form, but outcomes are negotiated with the tenant (F) so the settlement is rarely applied deterministically. Re-estimate H 5-10%, but disputes are a small fraction of reconciliations and the pool per landlord is tiny (H8).

Freight audit: finder's H 5% is fair, but the 'C 15%' accessorial-applicability bucket is where audit engines already convert settlements into contract rules the same day (H3); the addressable residual after the engine is mostly A and B. Re-estimate uncaptured H 1-3%.

Energy and telecom ombudsman complaints: finder's own split (A 35-40%, B 20%) already shows data errors dominate; the H 5% he retained is mostly the regulator's, not the supplier's. Supplier-level uncaptured H 1-3%.

verification.overall: The finder's structural conclusion survives adversarial review and is, if anything, too generous. Nothing numerical in this cluster could be verified by either the finder or the verifier: the session's search budget was exhausted before either ran a query, and every regulator, court, ombudsman, academic and vendor host, plus every alternative host tried (assets.publishing.service.gov.uk, law.cornell.edu, govinfo.gov, api.federalregister.gov, sec.gov, hal.science, op.europa.eu), was denied at the egress proxy. The only primary artefacts verified are the Procore developer docs (RFI tool as per-project archive; MCP read/write/converse tools; AI side-panel querying RFIs; a single 'official' flag on correspondence) and the DCSA standard (free time defined by reference to carrier website or service contract), all confirmed verbatim. Four finder claims are refuted: the pyprocore 'emerging AI RFI tooling' inference (one unofficial hobby SDK), the APS-SDK-implies-no-RFI-API inference, the 'only notion of an authoritative answer' claim about Procore, and the ~40% H share for FAA exemptions, which conflates routinised discretionary waivers of bright-line rules with repeatable ambiguity. The recalled Navigant RFI figures, AIA A201 structure, FMC 2020/OSRA sequence, MNE 14-month limit and Part 107 rule change are all consistent with the verifier's own recollection but remain unverified, and each carries a caveat the finder omitted (single-vendor 2013 data; contestability under A201 Article 15; non-exhaustive reasonableness standard; recurrence absorbed by statute). Honest H shares across the cluster are 0-5% at operating-company level; every genuine prospective loop found (FAA/EASA/AMOC/MMEL, FMC, MNE, Ofgem, Ofcom, code modifications) is regulator- or OEM-owned and already published and versioned (H3, H6), and the residual human work is missing facts, factual classification, discretion or negotiation (H1).
